fixes.explanation: Yes, married. The officers say, “Has any man become pledged to a woman and not married her? Let him return home, or he may die in battle and another man marry her.” (Deuteronomy 20:7) That's the third man on the list, after the house and the vineyard. Three men, three reasons to head home, and each one has something good he hasn't gotten to yet.

Yes, commanders. The text says, “When the officers have finished addressing the army, they are to appoint commanders to lead it.” (Deuteronomy 20:9) First the speeches, then somebody gets put in charge. By then the priest and the officers have both had their say, so lots of talking, and then somebody finally gets the clipboard.

Yes. The text says, “If they accept your offer of peace and open their gates, all the people there will become forced laborers to serve you.” (Deuteronomy 20:11) The offer of peace comes first in verse 10, and accepting it is the road that doesn't go through a siege. This is a heavier part of the passage, so I'll just say it plainly.

That's right. Moses says, “But if they refuse to make peace with you and wage war against you, lay siege to that city.” (Deuteronomy 20:12) The offer of peace comes first in verse 10. The siege is for a city that refuses and wages war. Offer first, siege second.

Moses says the opposite, friend. “…you must not destroy its trees by putting an axe to them, because you can eat their fruit. You must not cut them down.” (Deuteronomy 20:19) Even in a long siege, the fruit trees stay standing. He even asks, “Are the trees of the field human, that you should besiege them?” (Deuteronomy 20:19)

I get why that sounds tempting, but swords aren't the reason Moses gives here. He says not to be afraid because “…the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, is with you.” (Deuteronomy 20:1) The swords don't come into that verse. I'd be double-checking my own sword with a sweaty mustache, so I'm glad the reason isn't about the sword.

Moses doesn't promise that, friend. He does talk about a city that refuses peace and wages war in verse 12, but the reason he gives for not being afraid is “…the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, is with you.” (Deuteronomy 20:1) Nothing in that verse says the enemy will run. It says who is with Israel.

That's the one. Moses says that when they're about to go into battle, the priest is to come forward and address the army. (Deuteronomy 20:2) The officers speak after him, starting in verse 5. And the priest's message is, “…the LORD your God goes with you to fight for you against your enemies, to give you the victory.” (Deuteronomy 20:4)

Right. The officers ask, “Has any man built a new house and not dedicated it? Let him return home…” (Deuteronomy 20:5) The key is that he hasn't dedicated it yet. If he stays, they say, “…he may die in battle and another man dedicate it.” (Deuteronomy 20:5) So it's the man with the undedicated house who gets sent home.

Not quite, friend. The officers say, “Has any man become pledged to a woman and not married her?” (Deuteronomy 20:7) The question is whether he has married her yet. The passage doesn't say whether they've met, so the missing word is married.

The officers go the other way, friend. They say, “Is any man afraid or fainthearted? Let him return home…” (Deuteronomy 20:8) Nobody is told to stay and prove himself. The priest did tell the army, “Do not be fainthearted or afraid…” (Deuteronomy 20:3), but the officers' words to a man who is afraid are to send him home.

That's right. Moses says, “This is how you are to treat all the cities that are far away from you and do not belong to the nations nearby.” (Deuteronomy 20:15) That covers the offer of peace and what follows it. Then verse 16 turns to a different command, for the cities of the nations the LORD is giving Israel as an inheritance.

It's actually True, friend. Moses says, “This is how you are to treat all the cities that are far away from you and do not belong to the nations nearby.” (Deuteronomy 20:15) That covers the offer of peace and everything after it. A different command comes in verse 16, for the cities of the nations the LORD is giving Israel as an inheritance.
